newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Court hears challenge to British beef ban.
newsitem.headline: Court hears challenge to British beef ban.

text.p: The European Court of Justice in Luxembourg heard arguments on Wednesday from the United Kingdom and the British National Farmer's Union that the worldwide export ban on British beef should be lifted.

Britain and the NFU, in separate but joined cases, claimed that the European Commission exceeded its powers when it enacted the ban last year and argued that British beef poses no serious human health risk to merit a restriction on its trade.

Last year the court accepted that scientific evidence exists that reasonably links bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), otherwise known as mad cow disease, to a fatal human disease, known as Creuzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD). The highest incidence of BSE within the Community has been found in Britain.

The court ruled against Britain's request last July for interim measures to suspend the ban until a full hearing of the case could be presented. The court recognized the potential commercial damage to the British beef industry but found that the human health risk was too great to lift the ban.

Now the court is hearing Britain argue once again that the Commission did not have the power to impose a ban on exports of British beef to other member states of the European Union because they did it to bolster consumer confidence, not to protect public health.

Britain and the NFU told the court that prior to the ban the Commission had enacted measures limiting exports of British cattle within the European Union in order to protect against the spread of BSE, and said these measures went far enough. According to the NFU, a total ban was not necessary nor did it pursue a legitimate aim.

The Commission responded that in the past Britain had been given the benefit of the doubt, but that ever since the Spongiform Encephalopathy Advisory Committee (SEAC) found BSE is "most likely" to be a human pathogen, it could no longer allow the sale of British beef.

The Commission refuted Britain's argument that the ban was not a necessary protective measure by demonstrating that even Britain took extra precautionary measures after SEAC released its report linking BSE to CJD in 1996.
The Commission said it extended the ban to third countries to protect the Community from re-imports of British beef.

Britain argued that the Community could rely on existing protective measures dealing with imports of live bovine animals but the Commission responded that Britain's reasoning is flawed and based on the faulty assumption that SEAC's findings did not contain new information to prompt the Commission to take stronger measures.

BSE has been linked to the practice of feeding cattle with ground up cattle, sheep and goat meat and bone meal, or specified bovine offal. Although that practice has been banned in the European Union since 1994, the Commission suspects ongoing violations persist throughout much of the Community.

Last month, the Commission instigated legal action against France, Germany Italy, Spain, Portugal, Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg, Sweden and Finland for failing to respect EU animal feed production rules aimed at stamping out mad cow disease, including non-enforcement of feeding cattle animal byproducts.
The court is not expected to issue an Advocate's General opinion or a final judgment in these cases until the 1997-1998 term, which starts in September and runs through July 1998.
